title: Progymnasmata: Greek Textbooks of Prose Composition and Rhetoric
author: John Roche
summary: John Roche reviews George Kennedy's translation of the ancient progymnasmata, the graduated writing curriculum that carried students from fable and maxim through to full essays and speeches, and that shaped Greek, Roman and early Christian prose. His governing claim is vocational rather than bibliographic: a classical teacher is eventually called to reckon with the primary sources of what he teaches, and there is a difference between using a textbook and becoming the textbook for one's students. The review's most useful observation is that the four grammarians collected here, Theon, Hermogenes, Aphthonius and Nicolaus, disagreed with each other about the order of the exercises, some starting with fable and Theon with the shorter maxim. Roche reads that disagreement as permission, evidence that even in antiquity the sequence was adjusted for the child's benefit or the teacher's style. He also gathers their competing definitions of fable to show how much pedagogical insight sits in the variation. The verdict is qualified: the book is academic and offers no fresh reinterpretation, which is exactly why it belongs in a reference library beside a modern textbook rather than in place of one.
points: Roche's central distinction is between using a textbook and being the textbook, which he casts as an obligation of the classical teacher's ongoing formation.
The disagreement among the four ancient grammarians about exercise order is read as license for teachers to adapt the sequence to the student.
Four competing definitions of fable, from a fictitious story giving an image of truth to a false speech imaging truth, are used to show the pedagogical range inside a single exercise.
The review gives differentiated reading advice by role, recommending topical use for composition teachers and evaluative use for principals selecting a progymnasmata textbook.
Its stated limitation is the absence of any fresh interpretation, which Roche turns into the case for holding it as a primary source rather than a classroom text.
quotes: The textbook has its place, especially for classical educators who want, or are required, to follow a certain curriculum or a certain method that is perhaps ancient or outside of one’s degree or experience. The progymnasmata might be one such method, an ancient writing curriculum that gradually moves the child from simple writing exercises to complex essays and speeches.

There are many excellent textbooks out there that present an updated version of this ancient method, guiding both the teacher and the student through the exercises of prose composition and elementary rhetoric. However, as every classical teacher strives to be a life-long learner, cultivating the practice of studiousness and the appetite for wonder, there is a deep and profound calling to not just use a textbook but to be the textbook for the students.

The book comprises an introduction and five chapters with four chapters being a complete translation of an ancient grammar book (Theon, Hermogenes, Aphthonius, and Nicolaus) and the fifth book being an ancient commentary by John of Sardis. In the introduction, Kennedy provides a brief history of the progymnasmata (Greek for “preliminary exercises”), its variations, and its usage throughout history.

An incredibly helpful aspect of this book is to see not only how different grammarians explained the assignments and what examples they provided, but also how there was disagreement as to the progression of the assignments. For some, the exercises began with fables, since children are natural storytellers, where students take a fable of Aesop, expand it and flesh out the story. However, Theon would have the students first start with a proverb or maxim since it was shorter and easier for the student to write and then move on to the fable, which involved more writing.

Another value that this collection brings is the various insights and criteria for selecting readings for students to work with. For Theon, a fable “is a fictitious story giving an image of truth” (23). For Hermogenes, it brings the minds of students “into harmony for the better” (74).
With that said, the Progymnasmata: Greet Textbooks of Prose Composition and Rhetoric may be overwhelming for some, given its academic nature and format. But it is worth the effort.

Now, every book has its limitations, and what is lacking in this book is a fresh interpretation and presentation of this ancient and effective method of teaching writing. Despite Kennedy’s clear introduction and his thoroughness in presenting five ancient works on the progymnasmata, it is in no way the only book to own on the progymnasmata.
